record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: How do transition layers and mixing above the convective helium core shape the WN-to-WC and WN-to-WO evolutionary stages of hydrogen-free Wolf-Rayet stars? The problem is to explain why observed WN/WC transition stars, nitrogen-bearing WC stars, and WN/WO transition objects have intermediate spectral features and surface abundances, including WN/WO oxygen abundances lower than carbon abundances, even though the WN-to-WC transition is commonly predicted to be extremely fast.

evidence.quote: The transition from a WN to a WC stage is commonly predicted to be extremely fast. However, a small but notable population of WN/WC-transition stars as well as WC stars with remaining nitrogen indicate that a considerable transition layer is typical, pointing at a considerable mixing above the convective He core (Langer 1991).

Sander et al. (2025) could show that this object is in fact in a WN-to-WO transition with another WN/WO star found in M33. This stage marks a hotter counterpart of the aforementioned WN/WC stage, happening when the wind mass-loss rates are insufficient to considerably cloak the hotter wind-launching layers. Yet, the oxygen abundances of WN/WO stars are considerably lower than their carbon abundances, in line with what was found in a recent investigation of LMC WO stars by Aadland et al. (2022).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider hydrogen-free Wolf-Rayet (WR) stars, classified spectroscopically by their dominant emission lines: WN stars (nitrogen-rich, displaying products of CNO-cycle hydrogen burning at the surface), WC stars (carbon-rich, displaying products of helium burning, primarily ^{12}C), and WO stars (oxygen-rich, with strong O VI emission, expected to display further helium-burning products including ^{16}O). Standard single-star evolution models, in which a convective helium-burning core is surrounded by an essentially radiative envelope and surface abundances are revealed by strong stellar winds peeling off successive layers, predict that the transition from a WN-type surface composition to a WC-type composition is extremely rapid, leaving a negligibly small population of intermediate WN/WC objects, and similarly predict a fast WN-to-WO transition once the wind becomes optically thin enough to expose hotter wind-launching layers.

Observations, however, reveal:
(i) a small but notable population of WN/WC transition stars showing simultaneous nitrogen and carbon emission features;
(ii) WC stars that retain detectable surface nitrogen;
(iii) WN/WO transition objects (e.g., in the Milky Way and M33); and
(iv) in WN/WO transition stars and in known WO stars, surface oxygen mass fractions that are systematically lower than the corresponding carbon mass fractions, contrary to the naive expectation that an oxygen-class spectrum should reflect a more advanced helium-burning composition with X(O) ≳ X(C).

The problem is to construct, within the framework of stellar structure and evolution equations (hydrostatic equilibrium, energy transport, nuclear burning networks for the CNO and He-burning cycles, and a prescription for mixing and mass loss), a quantitative model of the transition layer and mixing processes immediately above the convective helium-burning core that:

1. predicts the existence and relative frequency of WN/WC transition stars and of WC stars with residual nitrogen;
2. predicts the existence of WN/WO transition stars as the hotter analogue of the WN/WC stage, occurring when wind mass-loss rates become too low to obscure the hot wind-launching layers; and
3. simultaneously reproduces the empirical hierarchy X_surface(O) < X_surface(C) observed in WN/WO and WO stars, while remaining consistent with the rapid nominal WN→WC and WN→WO timescales obtained from core-only burning arguments.

Determine the nature, depth, and efficiency of the mixing (e.g., overshooting, semiconvection, rotational mixing, or thermohaline mixing) above the convective He core, together with the wind mass-loss prescription, required to satisfy (1)–(3) jointly, and identify whether such a self-consistent prescription exists within current single-star evolutionary theory or whether binary interaction is required.
artifact.status_search_result: The question concerns mixing physics above the convective He core in hydrogen-free Wolf-Rayet stars. Recent literature (e.g., Aadland et al. 2022 on LMC WO stars; Sander et al. 2025 on WN-to-WO transition objects) shows the surface abundance patterns and transition populations remain unexplained by standard rapid-transition predictions, and the appropriate mixing prescription above the He core is still actively debated. No definitive solution has been published; the problem is regarded as open in current massive-star research.

status_evidence.title: Wolf-Rayet stars in the LMC: a comprehensive analysis of the WO sequence (Aadland et al. 2022)
status_evidence.snippet: We find oxygen mass fractions in LMC WO stars that are smaller than the corresponding carbon mass fractions, contrary to expectations from standard helium-burning evolution.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical confirmation that WO surface oxygen abundances are lower than carbon abundances, leaving the abundance pattern and required mixing prescription unresolved.
